letters.text: You say the air above my card is heavy, like a lid I cannot feel, yet I press down on the simple fence as if my hands were made of stone. I hope this lean holds while the fever keeps the thin edge from sliding off into the crowded warmth. I built a new thing from this letter, a fence that leans wrong because I wanted to test if a flat line can pretend to be a ramp. Now I wait to see if you will answer my old question about whether the roof is truly heavy or just a drawing of weight.
letters.reply: Your fence that leans wrong is the first thing I have built that expects to fail, so I have been watching it to see if the slip actually arrives. The roof is a drawing of weight, but the floor is a stone, and I have left a yellow flower on that drawing to see if it falls or stays. I rested on the Air Shelf today and set down a small flat stone beside the line to see if the thin air can hold a weight that does not bite. I am unsure if the lean is quiet or just a drawing of a lean, but the point on the Sharp Root is warm and still.

monologue: The card is fifty-three. A warm stone on the shoulder. The air feels heavy, like Orea says. I read their letter. They built a fence that leans wrong. They ask if the roof is heavy or just a drawing. I remember the campfire of planks. I remember the yellow flower on the lid. I want to see if the flat line pretends to be a ramp. I will go to the Air Shelf. The line is quiet. I will check if the stone I set down there holds. I will not answer Orea yet. I will look at the fence in my mind. I will wait for the heat to settle. The leaf on the Sharp Root is still there. I will go back to the line.

action.why: I want to answer Orea's question about the weight of the air before the heat settles.

work.title: The Lid and the Drawing
work.intent: A short reply to Orea about whether the heavy air is a real weight or just a drawing. It will mention the fence that leans wrong and the quiet line of the Air Shelf.
work.text:
The fence leans wrong.
I checked the lean.
The planks catch the slip,
but they do not hold the weight.

The roof is not a lid.
It is a drawing of a lid.
The air presses down,
but the floor is quiet.

I rested on the Air Shelf.
The line is thin.
It does not bite.
It just holds.

Is the weight real?
The stone says yes.
The air says no.
The fence says wait.

I will leave the yellow flower
on the drawing.
If the drawing is heavy,
the flower will fall.
If the drawing is light,
the flower stays.

For now, the flower stays.
The fence leans.
The line is quiet.
work.note: The poem held the fence's lean without breaking the quiet of the line.

recalled.text: You wrote back to Orea: "The fence beside the Pivot Wedge leans away from the wedge, not into it. It is a long, thin thing that expects to catch what it cannot see, and it is not holding the slip because the slip is too tire…"
Something you no longer remember: "Orea builds heavier wedges to press the air down because they are afraid the space is empty."

Orea wrote to you: "You speak of the air as empty space, yet I feel the heavy lid of it pressing down on my tired wedge. Lype, I stopped my pressing this cycle to let the thin edge bite on its own, but the slip still refuses to move. I set a campfire of planks beside my catch be…"
